title: Function Overloading

content.intro: This lesson turns the syllabus topic “Function Overloading” into a small, inspectable example. You will work from an expected behavior, run a local check, and record the assumptions behind the result.
content.why_it_matters: Function Overloading is part of the Solidity workflow covered here. Connect the term to a contract's inputs, state changes, external calls, or execution artifacts rather than memorizing syntax in isolation.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Function visibility determines who can call code. Mutability describes whether it reads or changes state, while modifiers express reusable preconditions.

items.title: Function Overloading
items.text: For this lesson, explain the term in your own words, identify where it affects contract behavior, and note one assumption or edge case to test.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Predict how the example should behave in relation to Function Overloading. 2. Compile it with the pinned compiler and inspect warnings. 3. Test one normal case and one boundary or failure case in a local EVM. 4. Record what the result demonstrates and what it does not establish about production safety.

content_blocks.expected_output: add(2, 3) returns 5. The function is pure because it reads or writes no contract state.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Paste the snippet into a local Remix VM workspace or a project with compiler 0.8.37, compile it, and test read/state-changing calls locally. Use only a local VM or test network; no mainnet deployment is required. CodeLeaf does not execute Solidity in the browser preview.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Reset the local VM or restart the test fixture, redeploy the example, and repeat the same tests. Restore the original compiler, optimizer, and EVM-target settings before comparing results. Never add keys or other secrets to source files.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: A snippet that compiles is not automatically correct or secure. Check the selected compiler version, read every warning, assert preconditions, test reverting and edge cases, and inspect external-call assumptions. If a tool or opcode is unsupported, verify the compiler release and target-chain support instead of weakening checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the small example to demonstrate Function Overloading. Write down the expected result before running it, add a normal test and a failure/boundary test, then note one design trade-off or security concern.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Function Overloading should be understood alongside the module principle: Function visibility determines who can call code. Mutability describes whether it reads or changes state, while modifiers express reusable preconditions. Continue to the next lesson only after you can explain the behavior, reproduce the result locally, and state the important limitations.

content.task: Create a small local-only example that demonstrates Function Overloading. Define a normal case and a boundary/failure case, predict the result, test both, and explain one limitation. Do not deploy this teaching exercise with real funds.
task_acceptance_criteria: State the expected behavior before testing and describe the observed result.
Include a repeatable test or manual trace covering a boundary or failure case.
Document one assumption, security concern, or version constraint rather than claiming production readiness.
hints: Start with the simplest behavior related to Function Overloading and make the input and expected result explicit.
Change one condition or input at a time and rerun the same test to isolate the effect.
Read compiler warnings and error details; do not treat deployment success as a security review.
content.expected_output: add(2, 3) returns 5. The function is pure because it reads or writes no contract state.
troubleshooting: Confirm that the compiler version is 0.8.37 and that build settings are recorded.
For a revert, inspect the precondition and test both allowed and denied inputs.
For external calls or network-specific features, confirm the local chain's behavior and the target-network assumptions.
